---
title: "Introduction"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-26"
format: docx
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

A growing body of evidence indicates that several psychiatric treatments, including electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), psychedelics including ketamine, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and antidepressants such as SSRIs, share a common mechanistic foundation: the enhancement of neuroplasticity. Despite their vastly different modes of delivery, each of these modalities has been shown to promote synaptic remodeling, upregulate neurotrophic signaling, and induce structural and functional changes in brain networks implicated in mood regulation. This convergence on neuroplasticity as a final common pathway has prompted a reconceptualization of these interventions not merely as neurotransmitter activity altering agents but as catalysts for neural circuit reorganization.

In clinical practice, however, no single plasticity-enhancing treatment consistently achieves satisfactory treatment outcome on its own. ECT, for example, can induce rapid remission in treatment-resistant depression, yet up to 84% of patients relapse within six months without maintenance pharmacotherapy [@sackeimEtAl2001]. Conversely, SSRIs provide sustained neuromodulation but often lack the potency to elicit response in more than half of all patients [@rush2020]. These limitations have led clinicians to combine treatments empirically—pairing ECT with antidepressants, ECT with rTMS, or psychedelics with intensive psychotherapy. Yet not all combination strategies produce the desired results. Some may be redundant, while others may even prove antagonistic. Timing and sequence also matter: when antidepressants were initiated concurrently with ECT rather than after its completion, remission rates were approximately 15% higher [@sackeimEtAl2009].

If combination strategies are to move beyond empirical trial-and-error, a deeper understanding of each treatment's unique mechanism is required: the specificity of its effects, the temporal dynamics of its action, and which phase of the treatment process it primarily serves—whether acute intervention, consolidation, or long-term maintenance. Each modality possesses distinct strengths and limitations. ECT and psychedelics deliver powerful but transient perturbations; rTMS offers spatial precision but requires cumulative sessions; SSRIs provide gentle, sustained scaffolding but lack disruptive force. Designing synergistic combinations demands a theoretical framework that can integrate these complementary profiles.

To date, no unified theoretical framework has been proposed that encompasses all plasticity-enhancing treatments. A useful starting point, however, can be found in the model of ECT proposed by Ousdal et al. [@ousdalEtAl2022]. They formulated ECT as a multiphase process of disruption, potentiation, and rewiring (DPR). In this model, a powerful perturbation temporarily destabilizes malfunctioning neural circuits, opening a window of heightened plasticity that provides conditions for the new neural configurations [@erchinger2023]. This conceptualization aligns naturally with the dynamical systems perspective on psychopathology, which views mental disorders as the system being trapped in pathological attractor states within a multidimensional state space [@schefferEtAl2024a; @schefferEtAl2024b]. From this vantage point, treatment resistance reflects entrapment in a deep pathological attractor, and relapse represents the system's return to that attractor after a temporary escape that was not sufficiently consolidated.

Yet the DPR model, as originally formulated, does not fully account for the maintenance of therapeutic gains. Even when disruption, potentiation, and rewiring successfully reconfigure the attractor landscape, the newly established healthy state remains fragile unless the brain's intrinsic capacity for self-regulation is restored. Homeostatic plasticity—the suite of compensatory mechanisms by which neurons and circuits maintain stable activity levels—may provide such stabilizing function [@turrigiano2011]. When homeostatic regulation is intact, the system can absorb minor perturbations without slipping back into pathological attractors. When it is compromised, even modest stressors can precipitate relapse. Accordingly, we extend the DPR framework by appending a fourth phase—homeostasis—and propose the Disruption–Potentiation–Rewiring–Homeostasis (DPRH) model.

The present paper advances a dual argument. First, we examine the theoretical plausibility of the DPRH model through the lens of dynamical systems theory and evidence from functional and structural connectivity studies. Second, we situate each plasticity-enhancing treatment—ECT, psychedelic-assisted therapy, rTMS, and SSRIs—within the DPRH framework, delineating the phase or phases that each modality primarily engages. On this basis, we develop a rationale for combination treatment design, arguing that optimal strategies should pair interventions whose temporal profiles and mechanistic strengths complement one another across the full DPRH sequence.
